utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning Your Honours, this is case number IT-03-67-PT, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Seselj, have you received our -- no, let's first start with the appearances, just to keep matters short. I see, for the Prosecution, it's Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, Mr. Saxon, and case manager, Ms. Katalinic. Good morning. You, Mr. Seselj, are present; and stand-by counsel present, Mr. Hooper and Mr. O'Shea, and the case manager, if I remember well, is Ms. Kulinowski. Good morning again, Mr. Seselj. Have you received our Scheduling Order in which you could have read that you are now representing yourself again?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received your Scheduling Order yesterday and I have an objection to its content. You say here in paragraph 1 that you ordered that the accused person be removed from the courtroom because of disruptive conduct. That's a lie. I was not removed because of disruptive conduct. I was removed because I requested that myself because I didn't want to be in the same courtroom with your spies, who are pretending to be my Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record, Mr. Seselj. You've also seen what the reason is for this Status Conference, it being that the Chamber would like to hear from you about your preparedness for trial. We are seeking another opportunity to make inquiries of you, Mr. Seselj, about your preparedness to commence the trial, and if there are any other matters, we would deal with them as well. So, therefore, I'd like to start, as the first item, to receive information from you about your readiness to commence the trial. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, I was trial-ready already on the 24th of February, 2003. Over these four years, you didn't do anything else but search for ways and means of effectively preventing me from defending myself. It is my right to represent myself and that is undeniable, and I'm not here on my own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, the Chamber would like to receive some information. I don't think at this time it is a moment for general statements. If you'd like to make more general statements, as far as your right to defend yourself is concerned, the Chamber will consider whether or not it will give you an opportunity to do so at another moment. The first thing I'd like to inform you about, before further discussing your preparedness for trial, is that, Mr. Seselj, you will have to familiarise yourself, and that could best be done with the assistance of the Registry, with the trial management procedures which would allow you to effectively conduct your own defence at trial. That would, for example, include, among other things, issues concerning translation of documents, as well as how to produce and how to present evidence in this courtroom. This is of specific importance because this trial will be conducted in what we call an e-court - that's an electronic court - environment. It is a system which is designed to enable the parties to submit and to possess evidence in electronic form, but an e-court trial does not necessarily mean that a trial is paperless. All of the Prosecution evidence will be presented electronically and will appear on the courtroom monitors. Usually, this would also apply to the Defence, and the registrar can assist you in learning more about that system. You don't have to use any of these electronic facilities; however, you'll have to present your material in advance, in translation, so that at least it can be introduced in the system to the benefit of all those who want to use that. That material will then be scanned so that it's electronically available. Therefore, that's of importance for you to know, that you should familiarise yourself with the procedures which will apply in such an environment. That's the first thing I'd like to inform you about. The second matter I'd like to raise is disclosure. I'd first like to verify whether you've received a recording, whether audio or video, of that Status Conference of last Wednesday, from the moment of -- well, the whole of the Status Conference, including the moments when you were not present in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a very serious problem there. In 2003, the then Pre-Trial Judge Wolfgang Schomburg, passed a decision that I be provided with recordings of all Status Conferences --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You haven't even got the patience to list to me, to hear me out, Mr. Orie. I'm telling you there's a problem there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, if you want to raise a problem, fine, but would you please first respond to my question. My question was whether you had received a recording of the Status Conference --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received a videotape and I don't know what's on it at all because my video player is down, doesn't work. I intervened with the prison authorities several times, telling them that they should get me another one, but they haven't done a thing about it. You are mistreating me in every conceivable way, wherever. How can I watch that when I haven't got a video player? As for the two Status Conferences held this summer, the Registry gave me forged recordings, where parts of the closed session are missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I'd first like to inquire into the ability you had to review the tape of last -- of this Wednesday. Mr. Registrar, is there anything known about the non-functioning of a video player and of any request by Mr. Seselj to have it repaired or ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the information that I received late last evening about whether Mr. Seselj had the opportunity to view the VHS tape that was sent to him, I received the information that Mr. Seselj had made requests to the United Nations Detention Unit in the past, but he was required to make a formal application in terms of putting in a request to receive a new video player to view the tapes. That has not happened. But I was also told that he has an opportunity to view the tape in another location if he so desires, but I'm not quite sure, at this point in time, whether Mr. Seselj has really availed of that situation. I need to make further inquiries, because it was rather late last evening that I got this information. So, as things stand at this point in time, there is information, at least to my knowledge, that the video player that Mr. Seselj uses is non-functional but he has not made the necessary application to request a new one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Seselj, this raises a few questions. My first question would be: Were you invited to make a formal application to have another video player available to you when you had established that it broke down?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I applied in writing as far back as May or June, and I sent back the recorder that -- the player that was not working, and what I got in return was another one that's broken. And I'm not going to write anymore applications about that. I'm not going to send you hundreds of applications about the same thing. On the other hand, you've been objecting that I've been sending in all these applications and motions and everything. It is for the prison authorities to check things that are being sent to the detainees, to see whether they are in proper order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I understand you well, that when the second video recorder or video player broke down, that you did not wish to make a further application in writing to have that one replaced.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You did not understand me properly. The second video player was not broken down in my cell; it actually arrived in my cell as it was already not working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My emphasis was on whether you did not wish to make a further application to have the one replaced, not where the video recorder broke down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the next application, I applied twice again orally to the warden; he promised that that would be taken care of. And then the third time, to a lady clerk at the prison; she promised that I'd get a new video player yesterday morning. And then during the course of the day, they came in, telling me that I had to submit an application in writing. Is this not maltreatment, Mr. Orie?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you going to follow that suggestion, Mr. Seselj, to make an application in writing for another video recorder?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. You should know, Mr. Orie, in law, an application -- an oral application is the same as an application in writing if it is presented in proper form, and to the authority in charge, just like you state your decisions here orally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's your view, Mr. Seselj. Next question: Was an opportunity given to you yesterday to view the tape of the Status Conference of this Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not have an opportunity because I do not have a functioning video player. I wanted to but I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At any other location than at the usual location, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No one ever mentioned another location, and I would not have accepted any other location. I am preparing my defence exclusively in my cell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's your view. Mr. Registrar, the Chamber would like to be informed about whether there are any reports that such an opportunity to view the video at any other location was given to Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'll make the necessary inquiries about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then hear from you later. Mr. Seselj, as far as disclosure is concerned, you earlier said you are ready for trial, but is there an issue of disclosure, anything at this moment you consider you would need for the start of the trial?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, I prepared seven points here stating my position regarding the commencement of trial. One of these questions is the question of disclosure; however, that is not the only question. All documents have to be disclosed to me in the Serbian language, and still, there is this practice that, in different ways, they've been trying to submit material to me in the English language. All documents have to be submitted to me on paper. Your Chamber ruled last summer that documents can be submitted to me in electronic form. It is the same thing as if you decided that had I to stand on my head in the courtroom. You cannot carry that decision through. You have to change it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, this Chamber took a decision, on the 4th of July. As far as I'm aware, no certificate for an appeal has been requested in relation to that decision, which means that that decision stands. I now do understand that you'd rather have it changed. At this moment, the Chamber has found no reasons to reconsider it, but if --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, that's not true. I submitted a certification for appeal and I also submitted at the same time the text of the appeal. First, the certification for appeal has been returned to me with the explanation that I did not have the right to appeal, and after that, the text of the appeal was returned to me as well, which I had submitted immediately, at the same time, in order to save time. You prevented me from filing an appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, is that because you filed it when counsel was imposed? Is that the reason? Then we'll have to look at this, to see whether another opportunity should be given.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, I submitted that appeal when you imposed counsel on me and I'm not going to submit one again. I cannot pay my legal advisors even for everything they've done so far, even without you maltreating me to submit the same appeals or files all over again. I will never accept anything in electronic form, and then deny me my right to defend myself, because I don't like to play with computers. You can do anything, Mr. Orie, because for you, legal principles do not exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, the Chamber will consider and further inquire into the steps you intended to take; that means when you took those steps or tried to take those steps, what caused these steps to fail at the time. We'll consider that in relation to our 4th of July decision and then we'll see what consequences should be attached to it. My first information, but please correct me when I'm wrong, Mr. Seselj, is that our decision of the 4th of July was received by you in a language you understand on the 7th of July. It is also known to this Chamber that counsel was imposed on the 21st of August of this year, which would mean that the time to request a certificate for an appeal had long elapsed when counsel was imposed. So the return of any filing in which you'd request a certificate for an appeal could not have been caused by the fact that counsel was imposed upon you because that decision had not yet been taken. So there must be other reasons. If you could inform us about those other reasons, for example, whether you went beyond the date limit or whether any abusive language was detected and, therefore, your application was sent back to you, please inform us. But --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Seselj, let me finish my line. But imposition of counsel could not have been the reason to return such an application to you. If you could inform us, please do so; if not, we'll continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, you know full well that I never use the wrong kind of language in my filings; however, as far as I remember correctly - I haven't got the paper there - the reason was the word count, that I did not count the words in the motion. I'm never going to count words. That's what my legal advisors do when they prepare documents for me because a computer does this automatically. But for me to do that kind of thing, no way, I'm never going to do that. And I asked that if you find that to be that important, you get a court official to count the words. Since you are duty-bound to provide me with resources, give me a word-counter, first and foremost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, first of all, you should have told us immediately that this filing was rejected because there was no word count on it. That would have saved us quite some time. That's one. Second, if you represent yourself, and if you submit anything, you are the one and the only one responsible for abiding with the rules, including rules of word counts to be in a submission. That, to be clear to you, if you find other people to do it for you before you file it, fine. You are the only one responsible for that if you represent yourself. Let's move on. You said you had a couple of points you wanted to raise. You talked about seven points, disclosure being one. I'd like to give you an opportunity to briefly present these seven issues so that the Chamber is aware of the totality of it, and I would very much like you to properly inform the Chamber and not, as you just did, give us the wrong impression that it was the imposition of counsel that would have caused rejection of your filing instead of the true reason, that is, the absence of the word count. Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, that's not true. That is the impression that you impose because you're the one who talked about counsel imposed, not me. I do not remember the text of the letter of the Registry explaining the rejection of my request for a certificate for an appeal. Perhaps it said "word count" or perhaps it said an "excessive number of words." I really haven't got the paper in front of me and I cannot remember all these details, because a normal person could not possibly remember all these details. Had you told me that we were going to discuss this, I could have brought the paper in and then you could have told me. And now what you are imposing on me is some kind of ill-intention, where that is far from the truth. Please allow me to present the other problems --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you have -- how much time do you think you would need to introduce the seven points?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hope that about 10 or 15 minutes will suffice, if you don't interrupt me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you will have 15 minutes to introduce your seven points, and whether or not I'll interrupt you mainly depends on the content of what you are telling us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you interrupt me, that would mean, Mr. Orie, that you will have to give me additional time. I know that it is your right to interrupt me, but if you grant me 15 minutes, then it's 15 minutes for me alone. First of all, I don't know what is the content of the indictment. I have been informed that you have asked the Registry to reduce the indictment and that the Registry responded. And it appeared in the press also. But I have not received the new amended text of the indictment, and I don't know what the outcome of your initiative is. If the indictment has, indeed, been reduced, then the pre-trial filing of the Prosecutor must also be reduced as well as the number of witnesses, the pre-trial brief. I think there were seven decisions, upon the request of the Prosecutor, for protective measures and you ruled that the names of those protected witnesses be disclosed to me 30 days before the beginning of trial. I still haven't received a single name of a protected witness. Number 3, my legal advisors have not been registered yet because the Registry insists my that my legal advisors have to fulfill criteria envisaged by the rules for Defence counsel. Legal advisors are not the same as legal counsel. I do not have the funds to hire the kind of people which will fulfill such criteria. I am satisfied with my legal advisors and they will continue to carry out very important work for me. I also need to have disclosed confidential documents. The detention management asked the Registry, the Registry agreed, and I was legally allowed to take out of the Detention Centre confidential material and they were never disclosed to the public. Now, suddenly, you are accusing me of making an offence by taking out confidential documents, and I didn't do that on my own. Also, I need to be able to have telephone conversations with my legal advisors and I need to have free visits by legal assistants and the head of the investigating team. Number 4, the question of participation in financing my defence hasn't been settled. I have provided all the information about my property and means, and the Registry continues to refuse to participate in my defence. I have lost a great deal of money and have acquired high debt during these four years. The Statute envisages the right to defence, and you can't side-step the Statute. Yes, you can have funds, but for Hooper or Van der Spoel or I don't know whom. I'm asking the Registry to approve the funds, and I will give a list of names of the people who have assisted me with their bank accounts and the actual amounts that they need to receive out of the total sum granted. Also, you haven't set a deadline for the pre-trial brief. According to 65 ter, this has to be at least three weeks before the Pre-Trial Conference. Also, under Rule 67(i)(b), on a number of occasions I have filed to the Prosecution the drafts of my separate defences. Only one has been translated so far, and I need everything to be translated before beginning of trial so that I can use this when examining witnesses of the Prosecution and witnesses for the Defence. Furthermore, I was not able to attend pre-trial statements and to examine witnesses under Rule 71. I was informed on a number of occasions, that an official of the secretariat has been appointed to do that, but I was never informed about the names of those witnesses, nor could I request to attend such investigations, nor could I express such a request to participate in depositions -- in such depositions. Therefore, all those depositions have to be annulled, as I didn't attend. Mr. Orie, I continue to insist that I should be in the front row of the Defence section so that the witnesses should see that I am on an equal footing in the proceedings as the Prosecution. I have managed to convey all my views in less than 10 minutes, Mr. Orie, and when you show patience, then I am able to complete what I have to say quickly and efficiently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seselj, you kept well within the time limits set. Thank you for that. Before we continue and before we might have some questions to you ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we might put some additional questions to you, Mr. Seselj, I would like to give an opportunity to the Prosecution to submit whatever it deems useful to submit in response to the issues raised by Mr. Seselj. Madam Uertz-Retzlaff or Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Two very short points, Your Honour. The accused mentioned that he "filed" a separate defence with the Prosecution pursuant to Rule 67. There was no filing. Several years ago, the accused disclosed to the Prosecution what he termed his "special defence," and the Prosecution is now in receipt of that. If the accused is concerned about having an English translation of that document, I can inform him and the Chamber that, to the best of my knowledge, a large portion of that special defence, and perhaps all of it - it was several hundred pages long - has been translated into the English language, so it will not be necessary for the Registry to take on that burden. Secondly, Your Honour, the accused mentioned alleged depositions performed pursuant to Rule 71 in which the accused was not present. Your Honour, the Prosecution has not performed any depositions at all in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Saxon, Rule 67 about additional disclosure gives an obligation to the Defence to notify the Prosecution of its intent to offer a defence of alibi or any other special defence. I do understand that you have been notified, although quite sometime ago, about the defence. And then, under Rule 67(A)(ii), the Prosecution is under an obligation to "notify the defence of the names of the witnesses that the Prosecutor intends to call in rebuttal of any defence plea of which the Prosecutor has received notice in accordance with paragraph (i) above." Have you notified, in response to the notification by the Defence, about the witnesses you intend to call in rebuttal of any of these pleas?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, we did not, Your Honour, because we did not consider these disclosures provided to us under Rule 67 to be any special defence, Your Honour, within the meaning of this Rule. They were simply hundreds of pages of quotations from the accused's books, copies of prior speeches, et cetera, et cetera. So we did not respond within the meaning of the rule. I've also been informed by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff that the accused has made additional submissions under Rule 67, but the Prosecution determined that it was not necessary to translate them because, again, they contained the same kinds of material - hundreds of hundreds of pages in the Serbian language of repeated publications of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. A question for you, Mr. Seselj, at this moment: When you notified the Prosecution of what, at least I understand, you considered to be special defences, either the defence of alibi or such special defence as the one mentioned, diminished or lack of mental responsibility, did you give the names and the addresses of witnesses and other evidence upon which you intended to rely to establish the alibi or the special defence? Was that included in your notification?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, clearly Mr. Saxon has not gained insight into this material. The material contains references to documented facts, and this material will be used by me most for the cross-examination of the Prosecution expert witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I'm going to stop you here because -- I will allow you to submit whatever is relevant, but you are invited first to respond to my question and then to add anything that you consider to be relevant. My question was whether the notification to the Prosecution included names and addresses of witnesses and other evidence upon which you intended to rely to establish that special defence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Not witnesses, but references to various documents, published books by Serbian, Croatian, Muslim, and western authors about various questions which are directly related to the indictment and the expert report that the Prosecution is preparing. Witnesses are not mentioned, but various books and documents, and it is clearly specified which book, which publisher, what page. This was an enormous amount of work. It took several years. And all that Mr. Saxon can say is that it consists of hundreds of pages. He is not at all familiar with the content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour, the Prosecution team had this material reviewed by persons who are fluent in the B/C/S language and we did not find any material that would fall within the scope of Rule 67. Just to give you an example, a lot of the material contained repeated allegations against the Pope of the Roman Catholic Church, and that kind of material, and we decided not to go any further with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, in the estimation, then, of the Prosecution, the submissions made by Mr. Seselj did not fulfill the criteria for special defence under Rule 67, but did you file anything with the Chamber to notify the Chamber of that view? Because whether it amounts to a special defence would ultimately be a matter for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, we did not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, that was about the Rule 67 notifications. I give you an opportunity to respond to other matters as well. You responded to the depositions under Rule 71. You said there were no depositions taken under Rule 71.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- if I just may move back to the issue of Rule 67.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I was not here at every single Status Conference over the last three years, but my colleague has informed me, to the best of her knowledge, we did say verbally on the record that we did not consider this material to fall within the scope of Rule 67. But we can check on that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we now have your response under Rule 71. Mr. Seselj, you said -- you referred to not having been able to be present at Rule 71 depositions and -- well, Mr. Saxon tells us that there are no Rule 71 depositions. Could you inform us on what makes you assume that there were Rule 71 depositions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On two or three occasions, the Registry informed me about the appointment of certain officers who will be taking these depositions. These were letters from the Registry that must be in the records of the Registry. That is a fact. Now, if no depositions were taken, all the better. But I have information from the Registry that persons were appointed for taking such depositions, and even, if I remember correctly, the dates were indicated, for instance, in Sarajevo or somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, is there a possibility that you have mixed up Rule 71 depositions with the appointment of a legal officer under what, at that time, was Rule 92 bis, to take a statement, which is not the same as a deposition, under Rule 71; that it was for the purpose of taking such statements which could be admitted later on by a decision of the Trial Chamber, be admitted into evidence? That you have mixed up these two proceedings and that actually there were no Rule 71 depositions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These rules are being changed at such speed, almost three times a year, that it is quite possible that you are right. But for me, what is important is that such depositions were not taken in my absence. But I think the Registry would be able to tell you that because I don't have all those papers on me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, therefore, at this moment we'll see whether there have been any Rule 71 depositions. Mr. Saxon, you have now responded to two out seven matters raised by Mr. Seselj. I invite you to proceed and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I don't have anything more to respond to at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Seselj, one of the issues you raised was that you did not know at this moment what the indictment was at this moment, and whether it had been changed or not. At the 65 ter Conference held on the 20th of October, the Chamber informed then counsel, the parties, of the following, and I'd like to update you in this respect. The senior legal officer said the following, he said: "In anticipation of the Trial Chamber's decision," which makes it clear that no final decision has been taken on the matter, "in anticipation of the Trial Chamber's decision on the Prosecution's response to the Trial Chamber's request to make proposals to reduce the scope of the indictment, I am permitted to inform you of the following: The Trial Chamber will conclude that the Prosecution shall remove Counts 2, 3, 5, 6, and 7 from the indictment. The Trial Chamber will also conclude that evidence shall not be presented in relation to the following: Western Slavonia, Brcko municipality, Bijeljina municipality, Boracko Jezero, Bjelasnica, and Bosanski Samac. This will not exclude, however, general evidence." That's the information that was provided to the parties at the 20th of October and is now provided to you. The Chamber still has to give a final decision on the proposals made by the Prosecution. Therefore, this is provisional information, as it was on the 20th of October, and it will soon result in a formal decision. It also may learn you that apart, perhaps, from some minor clarifications, factual clarifications, that it's mainly a reduction of the indictment rather than anything else. If you would have any need to comment on this or to make any submissions on what the Chamber informed the parties about in anticipation of its decision, then you'll have an opportunity to do so, not necessarily immediately now. But if you need more time -- you don't have to respond to that. It's mainly a reduction of the indictment that is in our minds rather than anything else. Yes. Then the protective measures you mentioned, I think you said that I --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I would just like to insist, when you complete your work, which I will not interfere with, I just insist that I get a fully modified text of the indictment - I think I am entitled to that - so that I have a clear text of the indictment. I don't want to interfere in your work. I'm not interested what I will be accused of. I just have to know what I am defending myself from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Rules are clear enough, Mr. Seselj. As soon as a decision has been given, an amended indictment will have to be filed and, of course, you will receive a copy of that filing so that you are fully informed. But this is just already for your information, what you could expect that will be omitted from the amended indictment. The protective measures, I just have to look up what you exactly said about that, if you give me one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seselj, I remember that you said that you had not received the names of witnesses 30 days in -- protected witnesses, 30 days in advance of the start of the trial. Of course, at this moment, it's not entirely clear when the trial will start, but the Chamber will give due consideration to that and will ensure that you receive the information in the time determined by the Court. Then, the third issue was about your legal advisors. That is, I would say, a matter which is primarily in the hands of the Registrar. This institution has adopted rules on who can act as counsel, rules about remuneration, rules as to what extent confidential information can be shared with others. These rules include qualifications of persons. This is primarily in the hands of the Registrar, and I take it that by now you know the procedures. There are a few matters pending as far as remuneration is concerned; that is clear. But I think that the admission of legal advisors, only in a situation where the Chamber is in a position to review a decision of the Registrar in this respect, that apart from that, that you should address the Registry. The same is true for at least visits. I saw this morning that you have asked for review of a recent decision of the Registrar on visits. The same is true as well as far as finance of the defence is concerned. But to the extent that finally the matters would affect the fairness of the trial, the Chamber may play a role there. As far as confidentiality of documents is concerned, it's not entirely clear to me what you said. Confidential documents, you said you were allowed to share them with others but they were still not made public. That's what I remember you said. But that's not clear to me. Could you please explain in more detail what you wanted to say at that moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, I have never illegally taken a confidential document from the Detention Centre. In 2003 and 2004, I think also in 2005, I regularly applied to the management of the Detention Centre and took out a number of confidential documents and videotapes. And this was intended for my legal advisor to assist me in my defence. The management asked for the approval of the Registry and such approval was received, so it was legally taken out; however, in these decisions of yours, it appears as if I illegally took from the prison a confidential document. Secondly, I must have at least two or three persons who will have access to those confidential documents and who will, on that basis, be able to participate in preparing my defence. Those persons have never disclosed to the public the content of those documents. I have, again, asked this Registry to appoint Zoran Krasic and Slavko Jerkovic as the persons that I will be able to hand those documents to, as they cooperate with me most closely in preparing my defence, and they are ready to sign a pledge that they will keep the documents confidential, fully aware of the consequences if they fail to do so. However, the Registry continues to claim that my assistants, members of my team, have to fulfill the criteria envisaged for Defence counsel; that they have to know English or French, that they have to be lawyers or law professors, members of bar associations, et cetera. I don't know by heart all the different criteria. My legal assistants need not fulfill such criteria. They are just assisting me. I am defending myself; they are not defending me. So this tendentious insistence on the part of the Registry is making my preparations for the defence extremely difficult. I can defend myself literally alone. You can isolate me and prevent all telephone communication and all visits. I will continue to defend myself. But you know what the legal consequences are of such an inadequate and inappropriate defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, first of all, you are invited to lower the volume of your voice a bit, if only for the very practical reason that if you speak that loudly, that we are not able to hear the interpretation anymore. Therefore, for that reason alone, if you want us to understand your words, we should be able to hear the interpretation of those words by our interpreters. So too loud a voice would prevent us from hearing the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try, Mr. Orie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, the confidentiality of documents, I think at this moment the assistance given to you and the limits is, as I said before, primarily in the hands of the Registrar. But the Chamber will certainly pay proper attention to it, what facilities you have, and to what extent you are or will be allowed to share confidential information with others. Where you said that our decision suggested that you illegally took out of the Detention Unit documents, what is most vivid on my mind is that reference was made to a telephone conversation in which I think you shared with one of the members of your team the name of a protected witness and that the language that followed caused serious concern to the Chamber. We'll further look into this matter. I'm not fully aware, and I think the Chamber would be interested to know exactly to what extent you are allowed to take out, with the consent of the Registrar, confidential documents and to give it to whom. We'll further consider that matter, but we need some time and some further information to further deal with it. Yes. Then the one issue remaining is that you say you should be able to sit at the front row if you are going to examine witnesses. Would you like to further elaborate on that, apart from what you've said already, that that's where counsel usually sits and therefore that's the place that you are entitled to sit in as well? And if that's your position, could you please give us, perhaps, some authorities, some legal authorities, for this specific question of being seated, if an accused represents himself, whether he should be in the position of an accused. If there is any case law or any practice you know of where an accused is allowed not to sit in the dock but rather to sit at the place where, usually, counsel sits, then we'd like to be informed about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is practice in most American courts. I don't know whether that is the case in all the states of the United States, but in most of them, yes. I am a trained lawyer, so I know that at least in part. In the U.S. system, the defence and the prosecution are fully equal parties to the proceedings, and visually, in the courtroom, they are on a footing of equality. The same bench for the prosecution; the same bench for the defence. They conduct the defence, and the prosecution, the same way. Now, why is that important for me? That exists in the American judicial system. I don't know, I'm not sure whether it exists in the British system. Why is that important? When a witness comes in here, a witness, who appears for the first time before a court, is usually a bit frightened; not always, but usually. Then they see you wearing that strange attire, and then if you are scowling a bit, then they are additionally frightened. And then there is the Prosecution, who is wearing these strange clothes, and then they were the ones who were preparing them, proofing them to testify. And then they see me, sitting here like a mouse, and from the very outset, this is a very important psychological moment that is treated seriously in every legal system, in every judicial system. I have to be on a footing of equality with the Prosecution. I guarantee, Mr. Orie, that no witness will ever be under any kind of threat from me. I will not use bad language. I will not insult them in any way. Perhaps I am just going to refute what they were saying, but that's different. But I, myself, have to feel that I am on a footing of equality with the Prosecution. Another important thing that I have to tell you in relation to what was said formerly, just a sentence or two. Do you allow me to say that, Mr. Orie?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A few moments ago, when we referred to the question of sending out confidential material, your decisions contained that question, too, and you were blaming me for things like that and that is why you were imposing counsel on me. The case that you referred to from last year was the case when I telephoned a friend of mine, a party member who is an official of the city government in Novi Sad, and told him the name of a person who is a criminal and a war profiteer. And I heard through the grapevine that he should appear as a protected witness in some of the trials in The Hague. I had no idea that he was meant to be a witness in my own trial, too. I never saw the man in my life. He was involved in business dealings with the city government in Novi Sad, this man. And during the previous -- the term of the previous government, he made a lot of money. So my suggestion to my party comrade was: Stop all dealings with this man. I will try to speak a bit more quietly. So when I spoke to Igor Mirovic, from Novi Sad, an associate of mine, I suggested to him that the city authorities should cease all deals with that man, that he should be fully removed from any kind of dealings.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the speaker please speak slower. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not only at our request a little bit less loud, Mr. Seselj, but also a bit slower because the interpreters cannot follow your speed of speech. Although there was no need to go into so much detail, the Chamber, of course, first of all, will pay proper attention to the fact whether you were put on notice that the person you were talking about was identified as a protected witness, but perhaps the Prosecution could tell us whether that's the case and where to find it, without going into any further details because otherwise we would have to go into private session. Or prepare for the next Status Conference to see whether we ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It would perhaps to be best to prepare that for the next Status Conference, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's one issue remaining. That's the filing of the pre-trial brief, Mr. Seselj. But perhaps first, the pre-trial brief was filed?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, the Prosecution has filed a first pre-trial brief, I believe, two years ago, followed by an addendum to the pre-trial brief, Your Honour, more recently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. Mr. Seselj, you said a pre-trial brief was due not later than three weeks before the start of the trial. Well, we have a pre-trial brief and an addendum to that so it's not entirely clear to me what your concern was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, you did not give me a deadline for a pre-trial brief. As far as I understood the Rules of Procedure, I also have to submit my own pre-trial brief at least three weeks before the pre-trial conference; however, I insist that the Prosecution now, if the indictment is diminished, that they should adapt their pre-trial brief to the reduced, diminished indictment so that my pre-trial brief would contain my observations, my responses, to what the pre-trial brief of the Prosecutor says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clear now, at least your argument is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Some matters still need further attention, Mr. Seselj, of your seven points. We are at this moment also looking more closely at disclosure issues, disclosure issues where we are trying to identify exactly what we have received, material which is not translated yet, I take it, but the information of the Chamber about disclosures of course, it's not -- all of it is not disclosed to us so, therefore, we need information in addition to what has been attached to the filings made so that we are fully informed about all disclosure issues of which, of course, the Defence is fully aware because everything that is disclosed goes directly to the Defence. I do understand that you have prepared material and that, informally, it has been sent to the legal staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour, and I also wanted to raise with the Chamber just so that there is a fair record of what has been prepared, whether you want to mark copies of these materials for identification in some way or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will discuss whether that's necessary or not, at least it should be transparent so that the accused is aware of what the Chamber received in this respect. This, of course, raises also the question of translation, well, some of the schemes, just the titles, translation of the titles would do whereas for others, it would not, although it seems not to be a very complex translation matter. The Chamber will consider and will inform you on whether we insist on a formal marking for identification but if you would already make available to the accused the material that you made available to the Chamber. I do know that it's not translated yet, so if the accused doesn't want to receive it, then it's up to him. Therefore, we'll further inform you about our position in this respect. As I said before, there are a few matters which need further attention. The Chamber will use the coming days to pay attention to those issues. Mr. Seselj, are there any other matters you would like to raise because they are relevant for the start of the trial, apart from the seven points, some of which we've dealt with already, some of which still need further consideration?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. A while ago, perhaps two or three weeks ago, the Prosecution falsely accused me of having done something through my wife, Jadranka Seselj; namely, disclosed the names of eight protected witnesses. And I never got any list of protected witnesses, so even if I wanted to do something like that, I could not have done it. That there was the possibility of having these witnesses intimidated, threatened, what have you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we move into private session, please, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll move into private session, and that also means, I take it, that the curtains should be perhaps -- perhaps closed session is better.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, we'll wait until we are in closed session and then we will continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in closed session now, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, first of all, I demand that you do not allow closed session on this occasion. I'm not going to mention anyone's name and I'm not going to refer to a single confidential document. I'm just talking about the improper and unlawful behaviour of the Prosecution. I cannot mention a single name because I haven't got any names. So I'm asking you now to go back into public session. There is no reason for having a closed session now, none whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, we remain, for the time being, in closed session, but we'll consider, after having heard and after having carefully studied all protective measures and after having verified whether, what has been said, or what then will have been said, doesn't in any way interfere with protective measures, we'll then consider to make that part of the transcript public, or not. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, I insist that all of this be made accessible to the public and you decide later, as you have concluded. What the Prosecution did, by falsely accusing me, was used as grounds for the Registry to impose restrictions with regard to further visits by my wife, Jadranka Seselj. Now I am discriminated against in relation to all other accused persons. Only the visit of my wife is being directly supervised and monitored. I want this discriminatory measure to be removed, and until it is removed, I'm not going to receive any visits, my wife, the priest, someone from the embassy. I don't want to see anyone. My wife never told anyone the names of any protected witnesses. Even if she wanted to, she couldn't have because she doesn't know them, just as I have not been informed as to who these protected witnesses are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I'm aware that a request for a review of that decision has been addressed to the President of this Tribunal. It is within his competence at this moment to see whether the factual grounds for such a decision are there. He is the one who will review that decision, as an administrative decision, and at this moment this Chamber is not competent to deal with the matter. Mr. Saxon, is there -- you asked for closed session. In view of what just has been said, is there any reason to insist on a closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary to continue in closed session, if this matter is now terminated, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but my question is also whether what has been said in closed session, whether that could be made public; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: To this point, yes, Your Honour, I believe it can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then return in open session, and in open session, I'll give the ruling that the closed session ruling does not apply anymore and that this part of the transcript could be made public.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber just ruled that where we went into closed session a couple of minutes ago, that on the basis of the content of what was said in closed session, there's no reason to keep that part of the transcript confidential and therefore it's public. Mr. Seselj, anything else you'd like to raise in relation to the preparation of the trial?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be all on my part. Just one more remark, Mr. Orie. A few moments ago, when Mr. Saxon spoke about the concept of my special defence, it is true that his colleague, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, mentioned that question here once, but it pertained only to the first filing of this nature which, indeed, had been translated into the English language. She never referred to any other ones. And this was a filing or motion from 2003 or the beginning of 2004 which, indeed, contains various quotations from different books of mine, but where I refute everything that the Prosecutor says in the indictment; that is to say, that the linch-pin of the indictment is that I committed war crimes through hate speech. And they refer to speeches I made, or rather, what I filed contains excerpts from my speeches made to volunteers, how they should treat prisoners of war properly, how they should treat civilians properly, buildings, property, and so on and so forth. That is what is contained in those speeches and in that material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, at least it's clear now that when you've notified the Prosecution of special defences, that you intended to rely exclusively on documentary evidence, not on witnesses and --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that you say once, but only on the basis of the first notification and not on the additional notification, the Prosecution mentioned it once. We can find that on the record, I take it, and that the addition you then gave to the Prosecution never caused them to respond to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, however, that recollection of the accused is not correct. I would simply refer the Chamber to the Status Conference of September 26th, 2005, transcript pages 418 to 419, where Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff made very clear the Prosecution's opinion regarding the accused's submissions of this so-called special defences, and there were several of them. Basically, these were almost pre-trial briefs in the forms of thousands and thousands of pages and were not any kind of special defence as reflected in Rule 67.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for drawing our attention to certain parts of the transcript. We'll review that and we'll come back to it at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, the next point I'd like to raise is whether your health and your conditions of detention, apart from the matter you just raised about visits, cause you to address the Court. And, of course, your position as a self-representing accused is a bit special, so we'll understand your words not only as representing yourself in your defence but also as an accused who is in detention at this moment. Is there anything you'd like to bring to our attention in this respect?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just insist that, with respect to detention conditions, I be granted everything that Mr. Milosevic had made available to him while he was representing himself, that is to say, an office, a separate office, the key to which I will carry in my pocket, where I will receive my associates from the Defence team, investigators and potential witnesses; and that that room should have a telephone and a fax. That is what Mr. Milosevic had while he was alive and while he was defending himself. He also had two adjacent cells connected. They did give me two cells, to be fair, but there's not an adjoining door, so every time I have to go to another cell, I have to ask the guard to unlock the door to that cell to me. This is not an excessive request for two cells. One cell will do. If I get this office with a telephone and a fax, that will be sufficient. But I will carry the key to that office in my pocket, just the way Mr. Milosevic did, the late Milosevic, until I die, too, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Seselj, I do understand that you request to be allowed to carry that key to that office in your pocket. This is a matter primarily, again, for the Registrar. Therefore, you first have to solicit the response of the Registry and to discuss with them, to make known your wishes, and then the Registrar will be the first responsible to take positions in this respect. And only once that has been done, the Chamber may be - may be - in a position to further deal with the matter, depending on what exactly is at stake. But it's on the record that you expressed here some wishes which the Chamber advises you to directly address to the Registrar, to start with. Is there any other matter, as far as health and detention conditions are concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for detention conditions, I have no other objections. But as for my health, drawing on the very bad experience I had when I addressed the Pre-Trial Judge, Mr. Agius, when I complained to him sometime towards the end of 2003, that for over three months I had been waiting for a very routine operation, and then after that, I was blamed in terms of having some kind of ill-intention, even in your decisions, because allegedly at that time I had already been informed that the surgery had already been scheduled. It was not official information; it was a nurse who just told me that, during the course of the following week, there may be an operation but it was not official notification. And that is why I decided --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that someone, if not myself, but I don't think so, has a mobile phone in this courtroom, at least I hear in my earphone, or perhaps just outside this courtroom. I'm not aware of it, but could you switch it off. They're not even allowed to be used in the courtroom. I draw the attention of everyone to that rule. Mr. Seselj, there is no need to revisit that matter on whether you did properly inform or did not properly inform at that time about a surgery that was already scheduled and whether we received this information from a nurse or from an official. I don't know what the rules there are, but there's no need to revisit that. Is there anything else in relation to your health which needs to be addressed?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, this was one of the arguments for denying me my procedural rights. For example, now, I could inform you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I'm going to stop you. A decision has been taken - and this was one of the considerations of the Chamber - that decision has reversed by the Appeals Chamber so, therefore, there is no need to revisit that. If it will play any role ever, in the future, we will see, we will come to that; but at this moment it's not an issue at stake. Anything else, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, if I were to inform you and your colleagues now that last summer, during some more thorough medical examinations, they found ulcers in the upper part of my stomach that I had never had before, and that I personally am convinced that, as for these ulcers in the upper part of my stomach, those were caused by you and your colleagues through your unlawful conduct, you could now use that as an argument against me, too, that I am behaving improperly. And that is why I'm not going to inform you about my health at all so that you would not additionally accuse me in this manner, because I wish to behave properly in the courtroom, not improperly, because my reputation depends on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, do you receive proper treatment for this medical problem you just told us about?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections as far as care in the prison is concerned. I did have objections with regard to the physician, but as far as the nurses are concerned, their work is really conducted in a very dedicated and proper way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think they will appreciate to hear your opinion about the quality of their work. Anything else, as far as health is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then -- Mr. Saxon, you're standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I know we need to rise very soon, Your Honour, if you will indulge the Prosecution for 30 seconds to move back to the seven points raised by Mr. Seselj. In one of his points, Mr. Seselj said that he has still not received the identity of protected witnesses. I just want to clarify with the Chamber that, in attempted disclosures made on the 4th -- on the 10th of July and the 24th of July, the Prosecution attempted, through the Registrar, to provide disclosure under Rule 66(A)(ii) which contained the identities of confidential witnesses, witnesses who had previously been given pseudonyms by this Chamber, and the accused rejected that disclosure. The second point very, very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just briefly respond to that. Mr. Seselj used that argument by saying, "I didn't know it." He didn't say -- he didn't complain about disclosure obligations met or not met. He said, "I was just not aware of it." What you are saying to us now is that when you tried to convey this information to Mr. Seselj, that he didn't receive it, so you're, more or less, supporting his view.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I am not trying to support his view. I am trying to say, Your Honour, that he had the opportunity to obtain this knowledge and he rejected it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if I have an opportunity to have some knowledge and if I don't take that opportunity, I might have difficulties in sharing that non-obtained knowledge with others. I think that's the issue raised. But let's go on to another point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I believe the point was raised in terms of his ability to prepare for trial, Your Honour, and that's why the Prosecution decided to respond, with great respect. One final point regarding the disclosure by the accused of confidential material to his legal advisors, at least one of these legal advisors is mentioned in the Prosecution's pre-trial brief as a person who could have been a member of the alleged joint criminal enterprise with the accused. That was Mr. Mirko Blagojevic. So the Prosecution would certainly object strongly to any such disclosure of confidential material to the so-called legal advisors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is clear. Then is there any other matter that either you, Mr. Seselj, or you, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, would like to raise at almost the end of this Status Conference? One second, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I never refused to receive a single document if it was in the Serbian language and in hard copy. If I refused any documents, then they must have been either in English or in an electronic form. And I really don't know what it is I rejected, because I do so automatically. But Mr. Saxon has now confirmed that I didn't know the name of a single protected witness. Mirko Blagojevic is the senior officer of the Serbian Radical Party, one of the highest members, and this is the first time that I hear that he belongs to some kind of joint criminal enterprise. He is not mentioned in my indictment. What does this mean? That you can say that all my associates are part of the joint criminal enterprise, the entire Radical Party? But I have confidence and trust only in members of the Serbian Radical Party. Then I can't have any legal advisors because all of them are allegedly part of this joint criminal enterprise. So I don't really understand this argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed. The positions are clear in this respect. Any other matter to be raised, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On my part, no, unless Mr. Saxon again says something so intelligent that I will have to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Chamber would like to have another Status Conference in order to further pay attention to some matters not yet resolved, and it is scheduled for Wednesday, the 8th of November, at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, in this same courtroom. We stand adjourned until the 8th of November.
